title: Ghost Market Is Pixar's Best Kind of Risk: a Specific Place With an Unfamiliar Door
dek: Pixar's newly confirmed March 2028 original follows a fast-talking child into a North Shore lunch shop serving stranded spirits. Its promise is not that ghosts are new, but that the doorway is culturally and geographically specific.
content:
## Pixar has finally put the market on the calendar

Pixar chief creative officer Pete Docter announced *Ghost Market* during Disney's D23 entertainment showcase on August 14. Disney's official account says the film will open theatrically in March 2028 and is directed by Trevor Jimenez and Jesse Andrews, with Becky Neiman-Cobb producing.

The premise is precise. ʻOno Market is a plate-lunch shop hidden on Oʻahu's North Shore. It serves lost spirits caught between life and death, and no living person has entered until a fast-talking child named Kyle blunders through the boundary. Footage shown inside the Honda Center introduced the shop and the supernatural adventure that follows.

Some of that information had circulated earlier in the year, when trade reporting described a Pixar project inspired by Asian stories about bazaars where the living and dead meet. D23 turned development reporting into a studio announcement, supplied the filmmakers, refined the setting and gave the film a release month. That difference matters. An idea is now a production with people responsible for making it specific.

## A plate-lunch shop is more interesting than a generic portal

Animation often enters fantasy through a door designed to be nowhere: an attic, a wardrobe, a glowing crack in a wall. *Ghost Market* begins with a business that could only be somewhere. Plate lunch carries the layered history of Hawaiʻi, shaped by plantation labor, migration and the everyday mixing of culinary traditions. The North Shore supplies another set of associations, many of them simplified by tourism into waves, beaches and escape.

Putting a spirit market inside that landscape creates useful friction. A lunch shop serves the living by routine: orders, portions, regular customers, food made quickly. A shop for lost spirits turns routine into ritual. Who cooks? What can the dead eat? What does payment mean for someone unable to move on? The premise creates story questions out of labor and hospitality rather than attaching local decoration to a universal portal.

It also makes accuracy part of the film's obligation. Hawaiʻi is not an empty mystical backdrop. The apostrophes and diacritical marks in ʻOno and Oʻahu are not design flourishes, and the region's stories are not interchangeable with a broad category called Asian myth. Specificity will have to survive development, marketing and the instinct to explain everything to a global audience.

## Trevor Jimenez knows how memory changes a room

Trevor Jimenez directed *Weekends*, the Oscar-nominated Pixar SparkShort about a child moving between the separate homes of divorced parents. The film's achievement is not plot complexity. It is the way ordinary rooms change under memory: a doorway becomes ominous, an object carries the temperature of an argument, and a child's understanding arrives through fragments rather than exposition.

That visual sensitivity fits a story about a place occupied by people who have not completed their journeys. A ghost market should not only be full of inventive spirits. It should feel like memory has altered the architecture. Jimenez has already shown that he can let emotion bend a physical environment without explaining the bend away.

Jesse Andrews brings a different experience. He wrote the novel and screenplay *Me and Earl and the Dying Girl* and is credited by Disney as a director of *Ghost Market* after work on Pixar's *Hoppers*. The pairing suggests that character comedy and melancholy will be designed together. That balance is familiar Pixar territory, but the directors' previous work may keep it from becoming a house formula.

## Becky Neiman-Cobb connects the risk to Bao

Producer Becky Neiman-Cobb won an Academy Award as producer of Domee Shi's short *Bao*. That film used food, family and a fantastical transformation without pausing to convert its cultural detail into a glossary. Its specificity was the source of its emotional clarity, not an obstacle to it.

That credit does not guarantee *Ghost Market* will solve every representational problem. It does show that the production has a leader with experience protecting a culturally specific premise inside Pixar's system. Producing matters here because the pressures arrive everywhere: story notes, casting, design, research, release strategy and the countless decisions that determine whether a setting remains lived-in or becomes a souvenir.

Docter's announcement also placed the film among sequels including *Incredibles 3* and *Coco 2*. An original film has to fight harder for instant recognition, but it gains something a sequel cannot buy. Viewers do not enter with a checklist of returning characters. The filmmakers can teach us how this place works one sensory detail at a time.

## Pixar needs originals that cannot be mistaken for exercises

The studio's recent strategy has been discussed as a contest between originals and franchises. That frame is too simple. An original title can still feel assembled from familiar pieces, while a sequel can discover a genuinely new form. The important distinction is whether the movie has a reason to exist beyond filling a date.

*Ghost Market* currently has one. The North Shore shop, plate lunch, trapped spirits and intrusive living child form a compact dramatic machine. Every element places pressure on the others. Kyle needs something from the market; the market has rules that his living presence disrupts; the spirits need more than a series of visual jokes if the phrase "stuck between life and death" is going to carry weight.

The danger is equally clear. Pixar has made several stories in which a young protagonist enters a metaphysical system and learns an emotional lesson from its inhabitants. If the market becomes another brightly labeled bureaucracy of the afterlife, the setting's specificity will have been spent on production design. The film needs mysteries that remain mysterious and local knowledge that is not reduced to a plot device.

## March 2028 is far away, but the standard is visible now

D23 audiences saw a clip; the public has an announcement and key art. That imbalance encourages overinterpretation, so the limits should be explicit. Disney has not announced a voice cast in the material available on August 18. It has not provided a full synopsis, and a short introduction cannot show how deeply the production's Hawaiʻi research runs.

What can be evaluated is the promise. Pixar has chosen an original theatrical film, two directors with distinct relationships to memory and character, a producer whose best-known work trusted cultural detail, and a setting too particular to disappear without anyone noticing.

That is the best kind of risk for the studio: not novelty as a slogan, but a door that could only stand in one place. *Ghost Market* will succeed if viewers remember the people who pass through it, the hands that keep it open and the reasons some spirits cannot leave—not merely that Pixar found a beautiful new shop to draw.
